concepts.decision: Select the form only after defining the recovery claim, impact tolerance, participants, and evidence required.
concepts.definition: An authorized examination of a DR plan or capability against explicit recovery criteria.
concepts.failureExample: A test with no criteria can complete without proving a business-relevant recovery capability.
concepts.label: DR Test

concepts.decision: Use for completeness, contact, and assumption defects when no behavioral or technical evidence is required.
concepts.definition: A review in which responsible people read and challenge plan content without rehearsing operational steps.
concepts.failureExample: It cannot establish that people can execute a handoff under time pressure.
concepts.label: Read Through

concepts.decision: Use to verify sequencing and ownership before committing alternate systems or production services.
concepts.definition: A procedural rehearsal that traces roles and steps through a recovery scenario.
concepts.failureExample: A walkthrough may expose a missing handoff but not a broken replication link.
concepts.label: Walkthrough

concepts.decision: Use when leaders need evidence of timely escalation, communication, and decision quality under uncertainty.
concepts.definition: A realistic scenario exercise using events or injects to test decisions and coordination without necessarily operating recovery infrastructure.
concepts.failureExample: A simulation cannot alone prove alternate hardware capacity or backup restorability.
concepts.label: Simulation

concepts.decision: Use for high-value technical proof when parallel resources, safe data handling, and reconciliation are available.
concepts.definition: A recovery exercise in which alternate capability runs while the production environment remains in service.
concepts.failureExample: If outputs are not reconciled, parallel processing can mask integrity defects.
concepts.label: Parallel Test

concepts.decision: Use only with executive authority, business consent, defined rollback, and communications because it carries the greatest disruption risk.
concepts.definition: A full-scale test that interrupts or transfers normal operations to exercise the real contingency response.
concepts.failureExample: A poorly planned interruption creates a real outage that obscures whether recovery would have succeeded.
concepts.label: Full Interruption

concepts.decision: Preserve expected-versus-actual results and unresolved limitations before declaring status.
concepts.definition: The objective-linked records—timelines, logs, outputs, decisions, and acceptance sign-off—showing what the DR test established.
concepts.failureExample: An attendance list proves participation, not recovery performance.
concepts.label: DR Test Evidence

concepts.decision: Create lessons after analyzing evidence and route material changes through ownership and controlled maintenance.
concepts.definition: Documented, supported insight from test outcomes that changes recovery plans, capability, or future test design.
concepts.failureExample: Repeating the same exercise without acting on evidence turns testing into ritual.
concepts.label: Lessons Learned

misconceptions.correction: A read-through proves shared understanding only; technical, dependency, timing, and business acceptance evidence require more realistic testing.

misconceptions.claim: A failed exercise is a failure of the team.
misconceptions.correction: A controlled failure is valuable evidence that reveals assumptions and improves the plan before a real disaster.

outcome: Given a recovery objective and test constraint, choose an appropriate exercise type, define success criteria and safety controls, capture results, and turn findings into verified improvements.

sections.body: A read-through checks shared understanding of a plan; a structured walkthrough rehearses roles and decisions; a simulation exercises responses to injects; a parallel test runs recovery capability alongside production; a full-interruption test deliberately transfers or stops production and carries the greatest operational risk. Select the type based on maturity, objectives, safety, dependencies, and tolerance for disruption, and define scope, authority, observers, communications, and stop criteria.
keyPoints: A tabletop can reveal coordination gaps without proving technical recovery.
Parallel and full-interruption tests provide stronger evidence but require careful authorization and rollback.
Tests should include suppliers, identity, keys, communications, facilities, and people where they are dependencies.
sections.title: Choose a test with a purpose

sections.body: Success criteria should trace to recovery objectives, service integrity, data currency, security controls, communications, decision time, and business acceptance. Capture expected versus actual results, assumptions, failures, workarounds, evidence, and residual risk without hiding uncomfortable outcomes. Assign corrective actions with owners and due dates, update plans and architecture, and retest material changes.
keyPoints: A passed exercise is evidence about the tested scope and conditions, not a guarantee of future recovery.
Findings need priority, owner, due date, and verification.
Lessons should update procedures, contacts, dependencies, training, contracts, or technology.
sections.title: Measure and close findings

summary: DR testing provides evidence that people, procedures, dependencies, technology, communications, and recovery objectives work together. A test should reveal gaps safely, not merely confirm that a plan was read.

assumptions: The scenario is a bounded application of the canonical unit, not a universal threshold, legal conclusion, or vendor prescription.
Directed edges carry only their printed relation; proximity and shared color do not imply ownership, authorization, or chronology.
Acceptance applies only to the stated scope and retained evidence; unknown or excluded conditions remain explicit.
